scenario: AITA for just being myself? | I'm (23M) British and have lived all my life in the UK up until recently, and I'd consider myself to be your typical Brit. I've always lived my life the way I've felt comfortable with and I try to stay true to myself. My humour and personality is very 'British', I make awful, dark jokes, I'll offend you, myself, everyone. Always joking and it's blatantly obvious but I'm serious and professional when I need to be, I support my friends no matter what, even if I constantly insult them. Almost everyone I know is like this, and I've lived in two different cities and been to uni so I know a wide variety of people. Never had any problem with it, I'm always open and honest about who I am. I've always thought this was perfectly normal. Almost everyone I would consider an acquaintance; male or female, young or old is more or less the same. I moved to the US 3 months ago for work on a 12-month contract with the option to extend it to permanent. I understand that the cultural differences are huge, but I just feel like I don't fit in at all. Everyone's so fucking nice and fake and woke. I'm young so for me the most important thing is to have fun and have a laugh. I can't do this here, the sense of humour is so shit and childish and unfunny. At first, I didn't really change my personality until I realised calling people cunts in a friendly manner within 10 minutes of meeting them isn't acceptable here, but that's fair enough, cultural differences and whatnot so I changed. I toned it down a lot but I still struggle to fit in, whether it's with colleagues or friends. I've made acquaintances with my flatmates' mates and about 10 of us were out for a drink and although I've toned my personality down so much, some of them pulled me up and said that they think I'm an AH and don't enjoy my company or my personality. A few others agreed and I feel shit now. My flatmates quite like my personality and said they far prefer the way I am to some of their other friends. One of them works with me and is one of about 3 colleagues that actually likes me. I don't want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven't had to before. I lost it at one of my colleagues yesterday after work who said 'yeah you're an AH and just can't be nice to people' because that's so untrue. My way of of being friendly and nice is by being a cunt, everyone back home knows that and are the same. I don't want to change who I am but I just feel I don't fit in - hardly anybody shares similar interests or humour. Americans can't drink so I can't even bond with people that way to maybe get them to see it's just who I am. Having seen how fake so many people are, I can guarantee I'm a more caring, loyal individual than most of them. They all love to talk the talk but at the end of the day, most of them are snakes anyway. I love my work and there's so so much more career potential for what I do in the US. I don't want to go back home but I feel I have to. Am I an AH for just being me?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.
Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Look for: - **Other expats** (especially British/European ones). - **People in similar fields** (your colleagues might be more open-minded). - **Humor groups** (improv, comedy nights—where "edgy" is the norm). - **Option 3: Accept the Trade-Off** – If you **must** stay for work, you might need to **tolerate** the social awkwardness. But this can lead to **burnout** if you’re constantly feeling out of place. **Hard Truth**: You’re not an AH, but if you **don’t adjust**, you’ll keep being labeled one. The US rewards **social adaptability**—not just talent. --- ### **5. The "I Don’t Want to Change" Trap** You say: > *"I don’t want to change who I am for other people, esp when I haven’t had to before."* But here’s the thing: **You *have* changed before.** - You **stopped calling people "cunts"**—that’s a **huge** adjustment. - You **tone down your humor**—that’s another change. The difference now is that **you’re resisting further adaptation**, but the US doesn’t work on "British time." If you want to **stay long-term**, you’ll need to **find a middle ground**. **Suggestion**: Instead of thinking *"I don’t want to change,"* think: *"I don’t want to **lose myself**, but I can **adapt my expression**."* --- ### **6. The Real Question: Are You an AH?** **No.** But you **are**: - **Misunderstood** (your humor isn’t "bad," it’s just **not for everyone**). - **Clashing with norms** (the US values **politeness and emotional safety** more than the UK). - **Possibly alienating people** (even if unintentionally) because your **default setting is "British," not "American."** **You’re not the problem—your approach is.** --- ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not an AH) + A Plan to Improve** You’re **not an asshole**, but you **need to adjust your strategy** to fit the US. Here’s how: 1. **Keep your core personality** (loyalty, humor, bluntness) but **reframe how you express it**. 2. **Observe and mimic** how Americans "tease" each other (often **less personal, more playful**). 3. **Find your people**—don’t force it with everyone.
